before_fields.label: Directory subsidies to Jacobin journalism
before_fields.meaning: The government discreetly assists selected Jacobin papers while royalism appears the more urgent danger.
before_fields.stance: Treat the subsidies as tactical management of political opinion rather than a principled adoption of Jacobinism.

SUBJ-SUCC-3F2B224B895F.label: Jacobins under the Directory: repeated revival, containment and repression
SUBJ-SUCC-3F2B224B895F.meaning: Clubs, press, constitutional circles and parliamentary campaigns revived in successive crises from 1795 to 1799. Governmental indulgence and subsidies alternated with closure, harassment and repression when mobilization threatened the propertied middle course.
SUBJ-SUCC-3F2B224B895F.stance: Pantheon, constitutional circles and Manège were distinct formations. Wartime emergency and anti-royalism created opportunities, but neither official encouragement nor electoral gains meant stable Jacobin control.

required_access_facets.label: Jacobins under the Directory: revival, controlled mobilization, and repression
required_access_facets.meaning: In 1795–1796 official indulgence and subsidies aided the press and Pantheon Club before closures and purges forced radicals underground. After Fructidor the constitutional circles rallied anti-royalists, then again faced restriction when demands for democracy and wider suffrage escaped government control.
required_access_facets.stance: The two cycles illustrate tactical use without empowerment of the left. Neither Jacobins nor constitutional circles were a uniform organization; distinguish Babouvist conspiracy, broad republican mobilization, and later parliamentary ambitions.

required_access_facets.label: Jacobin resurgence and emergency politics in 1799
required_access_facets.meaning: The post-Prairial revival of Jacobin newspapers, clubs, officeholding, and emergency legislation during renewed military danger, followed by Sieyes's containment of the movement.
required_access_facets.stance: The resurgence was real but did not command a parliamentary majority. Wartime emergency and memories of Year II magnified fear; Sieyes’s containment served his own executive project. Rejection of Jourdan’s Country in Danger motion marks the limit of renewed emergency government.

SUBJ-SUCC-032D51EDEC22.label: Babeuf and the Conspiracy of Equals
SUBJ-SUCC-032D51EDEC22.meaning: Babeuf interpreted the Revolution as class conflict and advocated state-administered common ownership and equal distribution. His Tribun du peuple and radical network joined a more broadly attractive demand for the 1793 constitution to a clandestine coup promising bread, land redistribution and punishment of rulers. Planned police and army subversion failed; betrayal, repression and the Vendôme trial ended the conspiracy.
SUBJ-SUCC-032D51EDEC22.stance: Attribute the class-war theory to Babeuf. The source calls him the first active modern exponent of full communism, but distinguishes that ultimate goal from the constitutional demand’s wider appeal. The conspiracy was organized, divided from other Jacobins at first, and coercive; do not equate every supporter with every leader’s violent proposal or treat military defection as achieved.

before_fields.label: Disintegration of the Second Coalition
before_fields.meaning: Austrian pursuit of separate territorial aims, Russian resentment, failed operations in Holland and Switzerland, and Paul I's withdrawal dissolved the coalition advantage.
before_fields.stance: The source attributes Bonaparte's opening less to French invincibility than to allied greed, division, and strategic failure.

SUBJ-SUCC-34E281DBB58D.label: Military crisis, recovery, and disintegration of the Second Coalition
SUBJ-SUCC-34E281DBB58D.meaning: The defeats of 1799, Novi and Joubert’s death intensified political crisis; recovery in the Netherlands and Switzerland changed the balance. Austrian and Russian rivalry, failed joint strategy, and Paul I’s withdrawal then broke the coalition advantage and opened Bonaparte’s military and diplomatic opportunity.
SUBJ-SUCC-34E281DBB58D.stance: French recovery mattered, but allied division and selfish aims also explain the opening. Do not present victory as uninterrupted or attribute all coalition failure to Bonaparte.

SUBJ-SUCC-3CA26E8D160A.label: Dismantling of the Terror and Revolutionary Government after Thermidor

required_access_facets.label: Danton and the Indulgents, campaign for moderation
required_access_facets.meaning: Danton and associated Indulgents pressed for less bloodshed and tighter central government, attacked autonomous terrorists, and became compromised by Fabre d'Églantine's corruption scandal and factional maneuvering. Desmoulins’s Vieux Cordelier publicized clemency and wrongful-detention claims with initial Robespierrist support. The short-lived committee of justice was abolished through Collot and Billaud’s opposition; Fabre’s fraud compromised the alliance.
required_access_facets.stance: Danton also sponsored emergency coercive measures in September; his later moderation and defense of Fabre did not erase earlier support for terror policy. Danton’s prior sponsorship of coercive measures and defense of compromised friends prevent a simple equation of indulgence with consistent principled innocence.

required_access_facets.label: Dantonists and Indulgents, purge and execution
required_access_facets.meaning: The prosecution of Fabre d'Eglantine, Danton, Desmoulins, and associates, including the politically broadened charges and curtailed trial. Amar’s delayed report and divided committees show that turning a corruption case into a political purge was contested. Danton was not himself charged with corruption; a misleading report of prisoner revolt enabled exclusion of defendants who had demanded witnesses.
required_access_facets.stance: The chapter emphasizes the vagueness of the accusations, the lack of reliable evidence for motive, and the purge's role in inaugurating the Republic of Virtue. Their potential influence is the author’s cautious explanation, not a demonstrated current conspiracy or settled account of every actor’s motive.
acceptable_access: Dantonists and Indulgents, purge and execution

before_fields.label: Electoral participation and abstention
before_fields.meaning: The elections drew unprecedented numbers into public affairs but turnout varied and was limited even in Paris.
before_fields.stance: The chapter rejects both a simple democratic triumph narrative and a dismissal of the elections as socially closed.

SUBJ-SUCC-AD1724EBE928.meaning: The elections combined broad but unequal male participation, indirect voting, local variation and political mobilization with sharply different rules and social outcomes for clergy, nobility and third estate. SUBJ-SUCC-AD1724EBE928.stance: Keep broad participation distinct from equal suffrage and representative social composition. The rules did not mechanically yield one unified programme; preserve named routes for each order and the franchise.

before_fields.label: Electoral qualifications and concealed oligarchic control
before_fields.meaning: The Assembly removed the visible silver-mark qualification for deputies while raising the wealth threshold for secondary electors who actually chose them.
before_fields.stance: The author calls the reform disingenuous because it appeared to democratize eligibility while placing decisive electoral leverage more securely with wealthy landowners.

SUBJ-SUCC-1C628235D449.label: Constitution of 1791: executive limits and the completed settlement
SUBJ-SUCC-1C628235D449.meaning: Constitution-making divided authority, restricted royal initiative and created an elective order before the final settlement after Varennes. Its operation rested on a monarch whose confidence in the Revolution had collapsed.
SUBJ-SUCC-1C628235D449.stance: Legal design and political legitimacy must be distinguished. Final acceptance did not erase the incompatibility between revolutionary sovereignty and the king’s rejection of its terms.

required_access_facets.label: Constitution of 1791: weak executive and separation of powers
required_access_facets.meaning: Constitution-makers subordinated a renamed King of the French to the legislature, limited the veto, separated ministers from deputies, and restricted executive initiative.
required_access_facets.stance: Fear of revived despotism and political distrust, not an abstractly balanced design, drove the unusually weak executive.

required_access_facets.label: Constitution of 1791 and the Constituent Assembly's settlement

required_access_facets.stance: The Assembly preserved its core 1789 design with limited conservative amendments; its institutional achievements endured, but it had already planted the divisions that would drive the Revolution further.

before_fields.label: Emigration waves and social composition, 1789–1791
before_fields.meaning: Successive waves of emigration followed popular violence, failed constitutional projects, religious policy, institutional abolition, military unrest, and Varennes, changing the movement’s size and composition.
before_fields.stance: Do not treat emigration as one aristocratic exodus or assume that every emigrant held the same program.

SUBJ-SUCC-7593EEA0BB95.label: Émigré counter-revolution: organization, foreign dependence and failed army
SUBJ-SUCC-7593EEA0BB95.meaning: The princes and émigrés attempted to organize propaganda, diplomatic support and military restoration. Successive emigrant waves, rank divisions, financial and logistical weakness, and dependence on foreign priorities obstructed coordinated action.
SUBJ-SUCC-7593EEA0BB95.stance: Do not treat émigrés as a homogeneous force or the agents of western peasant revolt. Their political claims exceeded resources and dependable foreign commitment; Condé’s survival was an exception to wider military collapse.
acceptable_access: Camps of Jalès and Catholic armed counter-revolution

required_access_facets.label: Organized counter-revolution and the émigré princes
required_access_facets.meaning: The emergence of émigré-led schemes for armed reversal of the Revolution, including Turin, the Jalès camps, the Lyons conspiracy, and the later base at Koblenz.
required_access_facets.stance: Early schemes lacked realism, secrecy, and a mass base; religious and sectarian conflict later supplied recruits, but the plots remained poorly coordinated and often embarrassed foreign hosts.
acceptable_access: Camps of Jalès and Catholic armed counter-revolution
Count d’Artois and émigré restoration plans
Émigré royalist counter-revolution: Artois, Calonne, Lyons, and Koblenz
Organized counter-revolution and the émigré princes

required_access_facets.label: Émigré counter-revolution: organization, army, and collapse
required_access_facets.meaning: Successive émigré waves built courts, committees, and an auxiliary army, retaining old hierarchies while accepting real personal sacrifices. Varennes accelerated officer emigration and militarization; the collapse after Valmy dispersed the main princely forces, leaving foreign-dependent remnants.
required_access_facets.stance: Neither a uniform aristocratic exodus nor an autonomous restoration army: sincere loyalty coexisted with status rivalry, logistical weakness, unrealistic expectations, and dependence on foreign strategy. The retreat after Valmy, rather than émigré participation in its cannonade, shattered the armed project.

SUBJ-SUCC-612D98E91089.label: Quiberon expedition of 1795: coordination failure, defeat and aftermath
SUBJ-SUCC-612D98E91089.meaning: The British-backed landing joined émigrés, prisoner recruits, chouans, supplies and royal authorization, but confused command, delays, discipline and Hoche’s response ended in defeat and executions.
SUBJ-SUCC-612D98E91089.stance: The fiasco exposed incompatible participants and defective coordination, not simply British betrayal or one man’s error; it also weakened Britain’s continental counter-revolutionary strategy.

required_access_facets.label: Quiberon expedition of 1795
required_access_facets.meaning: The failed British-backed landing of emigres intended to join royalist chouan forces in Brittany.
required_access_facets.stance: The expedition is treated as an ambitious fiasco that helped redirect British strategy toward colonial warfare.

required_access_facets.label: Quiberon expedition, 1795
required_access_facets.meaning: The British-backed landing of émigrés and French prisoners at Quiberon, its faulty assumptions and command, Hoche's victory, and the executions that followed.
required_access_facets.stance: Quiberon was the decisive, disastrously bungled effort to combine foreign power, émigrés, and popular rebels; its failure exposed their operational and political divisions.

SUBJ-SUCC-4F5D0E057A07.label: Condé’s surviving corps and Pichegru’s royalist contacts
SUBJ-SUCC-4F5D0E057A07.meaning: Condé’s corps survived the 1792 collapse in imperial service. Subsequent plans to combine it with Austrian forces, Lyonnais royalists, and Pichegru stalled amid negotiation and foreign caution; d’Antraigues’s later disclosures implicated Pichegru.
SUBJ-SUCC-4F5D0E057A07.stance: Survival in Austrian service did not provide independent Bourbon military capacity. Pichegru’s susceptibility and later implication did not mean that the proposed 1795 offensive took place.

before_fields.meaning: Emigres could return and receive amnesty if they accepted the permanent loss of property vested in the Republic, thereby separating personal reconciliation from restoration of the old social order.
before_fields.stance: The policy protects purchasers of national property more clearly than Louis XVIII had done and draws potential royalists toward the Consulate.

SUBJ-SUCC-DF287F758EED.label: Émigré return and irreversible revolutionary land transfers
SUBJ-SUCC-DF287F758EED.meaning: The Consulate's conditional reconciliation of emigres while irrevocably protecting purchasers of confiscated emigre and Church property.
SUBJ-SUCC-DF287F758EED.stance: Personal reconciliation did not restore old ownership: purchasers of confiscated émigré and Church lands remained protected. Papal acceptance of non-return was practical and did not concede the legality of confiscation or abandon the Avignon claim.

required_access_facets.label: Émigré return and irreversible revolutionary land transfers

required_access_facets.stance: Personal reconciliation did not restore old ownership: purchasers of confiscated émigré and Church lands remained protected. Papal acceptance of non-return was practical and did not concede the legality of confiscation or abandon the Avignon claim.

before_fields.label: Émigré royalist counter-revolution: Artois, Calonne, Lyons, and Koblenz
before_fields.meaning: Artois and Calonne planned armed restoration from exile, linked agents to Catholic unrest, failed in the Rhône and at Jalès, and relocated the émigré court from Turin to Koblenz.
before_fields.stance: The author depicts the network as unrealistic and insecure but increasingly connected to domestic religious conflict.
acceptable_access: Émigré royalist counter-revolution: Artois, Calonne, Lyons, and Koblenz

SUBJ-SUCC-7593EEA0BB95.label: Émigré counter-revolution: organization, foreign dependence and failed army
SUBJ-SUCC-7593EEA0BB95.meaning: The princes and émigrés attempted to organize propaganda, diplomatic support and military restoration. Successive emigrant waves, rank divisions, financial and logistical weakness, and dependence on foreign priorities obstructed coordinated action.
SUBJ-SUCC-7593EEA0BB95.stance: Do not treat émigrés as a homogeneous force or the agents of western peasant revolt. Their political claims exceeded resources and dependable foreign commitment; Condé’s survival was an exception to wider military collapse.

required_access_facets.label: Organized counter-revolution and the émigré princes
required_access_facets.meaning: The emergence of émigré-led schemes for armed reversal of the Revolution, including Turin, the Jalès camps, the Lyons conspiracy, and the later base at Koblenz.
required_access_facets.stance: Early schemes lacked realism, secrecy, and a mass base; religious and sectarian conflict later supplied recruits, but the plots remained poorly coordinated and often embarrassed foreign hosts.
acceptable_access: Camps of Jalès and Catholic armed counter-revolution
Count d’Artois and émigré restoration plans
Émigré royalist counter-revolution: Artois, Calonne, Lyons, and Koblenz
Organized counter-revolution and the émigré princes

required_access_facets.label: Émigré counter-revolution: organization, army, and collapse
required_access_facets.meaning: Successive émigré waves built courts, committees, and an auxiliary army, retaining old hierarchies while accepting real personal sacrifices. Varennes accelerated officer emigration and militarization; the collapse after Valmy dispersed the main princely forces, leaving foreign-dependent remnants.
required_access_facets.stance: Neither a uniform aristocratic exodus nor an autonomous restoration army: sincere loyalty coexisted with status rivalry, logistical weakness, unrealistic expectations, and dependence on foreign strategy. The retreat after Valmy, rather than émigré participation in its cannonade, shattered the armed project.

before_fields.label: Emigres: emigration, decrees, and war pretext
before_fields.meaning: Continuing emigration, armed organization abroad, punitive legislation, royal resistance, and pressure on German rulers converted a domestic opposition problem into a route toward war.
before_fields.stance: The chapter distinguishes the emigres' symbolic and political importance from Robespierre's judgment that they were less dangerous than domestic counter-revolutionaries.

before_fields.label: Encyclopédie—mass reception, notoriety, and the culture of encyclopedism
before_fields.meaning: Expanded editions and smaller formats created a large market; notoriety, irreverence, and contempt for authority made the work influential, while encyclopedism came to signify independent judgment.
before_fields.stance: Recognize both the work's reference quality and the anti-authoritarian reputation that chiefly drove sales.

before_fields.label: End of the revolutionary paper-money experiment
before_fields.meaning: Official demonetization of territorial mandates in February 1797 closes the paper-money system begun with assignats.
before_fields.stance: Treat this as a monetary endpoint that immediately creates a new deflationary crisis rather than restoring normal finance.
acceptable_access: End of the revolutionary paper-money experiment

SUBJ-SUCC-5193E3F37320.label: Assignats: land-backed origins, paper currency, inflation and redistribution
SUBJ-SUCC-5193E3F37320.meaning: Nationalized land supported an initial bond scheme that became circulating paper. Over-issue, fiscal weakness and war drove depreciation, altered national-land sale returns and redistributed resources among debtors, creditors, wage earners and purchasers.
SUBJ-SUCC-5193E3F37320.stance: Distinguish the original retirement-through-land-sales plan from later monetary practice. War intensified rather than alone caused depreciation; nominal payment or cheap acquisition cannot be treated as equivalent real value.
acceptable_access: Assignats: land-backed bonds becoming paper money
John Law's legacy and distrust of banks and financiers
National lands and the Extraordinary Fund

required_access_facets.label: Assignats: origin as land-backed bonds and conversion into paper money
required_access_facets.meaning: Assignats began as interest-bearing bonds secured on national lands and usable to buy them, then became legal tender and multiplied rapidly to cover widening deficits and compensation.
required_access_facets.stance: Keep successive institutional and monetary forms distinct; land security did not remove risks or the need for further issues.
acceptable_access: Assignats: land-backed bonds becoming paper money
John Law's legacy and distrust of banks and financiers
National lands and the Extraordinary Fund

required_access_facets.label: Assignats, inflation, and fiscal breakdown
required_access_facets.meaning: The accelerating depreciation of assignats and weakening state finance during the winter and spring of 1794-1795.
required_access_facets.stance: Currency collapse is presented as both a cause and consequence of market liberalization, harvest shortage, and wartime procurement needs.

required_access_facets.label: Assignats, inflation, and redistribution between debtors and creditors
required_access_facets.meaning: Over-issued land-backed assignats depreciated severely, undermining land-sale returns, credit, fixed incomes, wages, production, and employment.
required_access_facets.stance: War intensified the monetary collapse, but fiscal weakness and revolutionary over-issue caused most depreciation and broad economic damage.

required_access_facets.label: Assignats: final collapse and abandonment
required_access_facets.meaning: Further depreciation, failed emergency levies and opposition to a land bank culminated in the end of assignat printing. Symbolic destruction of the plates did not itself restore finance.
required_access_facets.stance: Distinguish the ending of assignat production from the later failure of mandates and the deflation caused by scarce metallic currency.

SUBJ-SUCC-F6EDFC76AB9A.label: Territorial mandates and post-paper deflation
SUBJ-SUCC-F6EDFC76AB9A.meaning: Land-backed mandates rapidly depreciated and facilitated property speculation before losing legal-tender status and being demonetized. Scarce specie then brought falling prices, high interest, pressure on debtors and barter.
SUBJ-SUCC-F6EDFC76AB9A.stance: A new name and land backing did not stabilize paper. Ending paper money replaced inflation with a different crisis rather than normal monetary conditions.

SUBJ-SUCC-8B341BCAF68F.stance: Its opening impetus was more intellectual than social or economic, and its leaders sincerely understood themselves as agents of Enlightenment progress.

before_fields.label: Enragés: suppression by victorious radicals
before_fields.meaning: The arrest or disappearance of Roux, Varlet, and Leclerc after Hébertist and Montagnard rivals adopted much of their economic program.
before_fields.stance: The radicals eliminated competitors whose policies they had appropriated; suppression also ended the enragés' demand to activate the democratic constitution.

SUBJ-SUCC-FEC4961768F7.label: Enragés: social demands and suppression
SUBJ-SUCC-FEC4961768F7.meaning: Roux, Varlet and associated militants challenged economic hardship and the limits of representative government through subsistence and popular-sovereignty demands before being marginalized and suppressed.
SUBJ-SUCC-FEC4961768F7.stance: Their pressure influenced radical politics but they were neither a coherent national party nor identical with Hébertists or all sansculottes.
acceptable_access: Enragés - economic demands and political role

required_access_facets.label: Enragés, Roux, and Varlet
required_access_facets.meaning: Roux, Varlet, and associated militants pressed for direct popular action, punishment of hoarders, and deeper purges, challenging representative government and later the Montagnards themselves.
required_access_facets.stance: The source says there was probably no plot behind 25 February; this is a qualified inference, not proof of absence. Roux and Varlet articulated real grievances and challenged representation, then faced Montagnard suppression.
acceptable_access: Enragés - economic demands and political role

required_access_facets.label: Enragés, program and suppression
required_access_facets.meaning: Roux, Varlet, and Leclerc pressed for radical subsistence, anti-hoarding, and democratic measures before Hébertists appropriated their program and had them arrested or silenced.
required_access_facets.stance: Their policies substantially overlapped later official radicalism; their disappearance reflected political elimination rather than resolution of their grievances.

before_fields.label: Episcopal reset: constitutional and refractory churches
before_fields.meaning: The Revolution left rival constitutional and refractory hierarchies; the settlement required displacement of all existing bishops and creation of a new bench.
before_fields.stance: The Pope's removal of refractory bishops enhanced papal authority, while Bonaparte's nomination of some constitutional clergy denied a simple royalist restoration.
acceptable_access: Episcopal reset: constitutional and refractory churches

SUBJ-SUCC-F1FC19003FE5.label: Organic Articles, Gallican controls, and episcopal reorganization
SUBJ-SUCC-F1FC19003FE5.meaning: The removal of constitutional and refractory bishops, appointment of a new mixed episcopate, and unilateral Organic Articles restricting papal authority in France.
SUBJ-SUCC-F1FC19003FE5.stance: The settlement gives the Pope unprecedented recognition yet subjects the French Church to stronger Gallican and administrative control, with unresolved tensions accepted to preserve the larger agreement.
acceptable_access: Papal authority--spiritual recognition and Gallican restraint

required_access_facets.label: Organic Articles, Gallican controls, and episcopal reorganization

SUBJ-SUCC-0848F7E708D9.label: Concordat: negotiated settlement, papal revival and lasting polarization
SUBJ-SUCC-0848F7E708D9.meaning: Bonaparte and Pius VII restored public Catholic worship and a reorganized paid hierarchy while protecting religious freedom, state nomination and revolutionary property transfers. Papal spiritual authority gained recognition even as the Church remained poorer and subject to state controls; memories of schism and persecution sustained later Catholic-republican conflict.
SUBJ-SUCC-0848F7E708D9.stance: The settlement was a difficult compromise, not old-regime restoration or a simple French diktat. It reconciled major institutions without erasing every religious division, and the papacy’s gain coexisted with Gallican restrictions and eventual political separation.
acceptable_access: Catholic majority religion versus exclusive state religion

required_access_facets.label: Concordat of 1801: negotiation and settlement
required_access_facets.meaning: The difficult agreement between Bonaparte and Pius VII that restored public Catholic worship and a salaried hierarchy while preserving revolutionary religious liberty and state control.
required_access_facets.stance: The Concordat was a difficult bargain, not a dictated peace. Catholicism was recognized as the majority faith without abolishing other beliefs; paid clergy, state nomination and oaths linked restored worship to government. Neither old-regime restoration nor Jacobin separation prevailed, and property transfers remained secure.
acceptable_access: Catholic majority religion versus exclusive state religion

required_access_facets.label: Concordat, papal revival, and Church–republican polarization
required_access_facets.meaning: The Concordat restored worship and papal authority without restoring the old Church, while the revolutionary religious quarrel hardened Catholic and republican antagonism through 1905.
required_access_facets.stance: The papacy paradoxically gained authority from revolutionary persecution, but reconciliation remained incomplete and politically polarizing.

before_fields.label: Equals' insurrectionary programme
before_fields.meaning: The printed plan promises the Constitution of 1793, free bread, redistribution of national land under the Ventôse laws, and punishment of alleged usurpers.
before_fields.stance: Preserve the combined democratic, subsistence, redistributive, and punitive elements rather than reducing the plot to property abolition alone.

SUBJ-SUCC-032D51EDEC22.label: Babeuf and the Conspiracy of Equals
SUBJ-SUCC-032D51EDEC22.meaning: Babeuf interpreted the Revolution as class conflict and advocated state-administered common ownership and equal distribution. His Tribun du peuple and radical network joined a more broadly attractive demand for the 1793 constitution to a clandestine coup promising bread, land redistribution and punishment of rulers. Planned police and army subversion failed; betrayal, repression and the Vendôme trial ended the conspiracy.
SUBJ-SUCC-032D51EDEC22.stance: Attribute the class-war theory to Babeuf. The source calls him the first active modern exponent of full communism, but distinguishes that ultimate goal from the constitutional demand’s wider appeal. The conspiracy was organized, divided from other Jacobins at first, and coercive; do not equate every supporter with every leader’s violent proposal or treat military defection as achieved.

before_fields.label: Estates-General as the demanded and ultimately scheduled remedy
before_fields.meaning: Once elite and judicial opponents denied the Crown's authority to create new taxes, the Estates-General became the accepted national body for consent, constitutional settlement, and recovery, culminating in a fixed meeting date for 1789.
before_fields.stance: Preserve the changing function of the demand: Calonne first rejected the body as unpredictable, opponents then invoked it to deny tax authority, Brienne attempted to defer and manage it, and insolvency finally forced a definite convocation.

SUBJ-SUCC-27DFBAFAABE0.label: Estates-General: emergence as the demanded constitutional remedy

SUBJ-SUCC-27DFBAFAABE0.stance: The source treats the demand as both popular and destabilizing: ministers attempted to defer, co-opt, or manipulate it before bankruptcy forced a definite meeting date.

required_access_facets.label: Revolutionary Government, creation and centralization
required_access_facets.meaning: Emergency government evolved from a formally limited Committee of Public Safety into a centralized revolutionary state directing administration, police, and enforcement while remaining under the Convention. The Law of 14 Frimaire made the Convention paramount, required district and commune reports through national agents, bypassed departmental political authority and abolished local armies. Robespierre distinguished temporary revolutionary government from constitutional protection.
required_access_facets.stance: Do not equate the Committee with an uncontested conventional executive; the source stresses both its growing practical leadership and the Convention's overriding authority. Administrative implementation took months; Javogues resisted recall, and formal centralization is not proof of instantaneous obedience.

required_access_facets.label: The 'Federalist' revolt: character, motives, and limits
required_access_facets.meaning: The dispersed provincial revolts of 1793 joined republican resistance to Parisian and Montagnard domination with local social conflict, property fears, wartime burdens, and limited royalist opportunism. Rich leaders required ordinary workers’ support; shared insecurity and reluctance to leave home also explain the departmental armies’ poor recruitment and collapse. Marseilles’s example spread unevenly through the Midi, while some frontier cities declined to commit.
required_access_facets.stance: The label 'Federalist' is retained as a contested contemporary label; the movement generally defended a unified republic and local autonomy, was geographically narrower than panic suggested, and failed through division and weak military commitment. Neither a purely bourgeois class reaction nor a single royalist plan captures the temporary coalitions; the eight-department contemporary assessment is a corrective to inflated claims rather than an exact timeless measure.

required_access_facets.label: Assignats, inflation, and fiscal breakdown

required_access_facets.stance: Currency collapse is presented as both a cause and consequence of market liberalization, harvest shortage, and wartime procurement needs.

required_access_facets.label: Assignats, inflation, and redistribution between debtors and creditors
required_access_facets.meaning: Over-issued land-backed assignats depreciated severely, undermining land-sale returns, credit, fixed incomes, wages, production, and employment.
required_access_facets.stance: War intensified the monetary collapse, but fiscal weakness and revolutionary over-issue caused most depreciation and broad economic damage.

required_access_facets.label: Assignats: final collapse and abandonment

required_access_facets.stance: Distinguish the ending of assignat production from the later failure of mandates and the deflation caused by scarce metallic currency.

SUBJ-SUCC-F6EDFC76AB9A.label: Territorial mandates and post-paper deflation

SUBJ-SUCC-F6EDFC76AB9A.stance: A new name and land backing did not stabilize paper. Ending paper money replaced inflation with a different crisis rather than normal monetary conditions.

before_fields.label: Failure of Anglo-French peace in 1797
before_fields.meaning: Britain was prepared to recognize French European gains and return French colonial captures, but France demanded restoration of Dutch and Spanish colonial losses without compensation.
before_fields.stance: The Directory sought total surrender after Fructidor; Pitt's refusal rested on remaining maritime leverage rather than unwillingness to compromise at all.

SUBJ-SUCC-2E013F69DF56.label: Lille negotiations, Fructidor, and the hardening of French peace terms
SUBJ-SUCC-2E013F69DF56.meaning: British peace efforts developed from the failed 1796 mission to Lille in 1797 as Pitt adapted to allied defeats and strategic stalemate. Royalist and moderate gains initially offered room for compromise; Fructidor removed them and hardened French terms. Britain accepted French European gains but rejected uncompensated restitution of Dutch and Spanish colonial captures as well as French possessions.
SUBJ-SUCC-2E013F69DF56.stance: Pitt’s willingness to negotiate was real but bounded by remaining maritime strength; the breakdown cannot be reduced to ideological refusal of peace.

required_access_facets.label: The 'Federalist' revolt: character, motives, and limits
required_access_facets.meaning: The dispersed provincial revolts of 1793 joined republican resistance to Parisian and Montagnard domination with local social conflict, property fears, wartime burdens, and limited royalist opportunism. Rich leaders required ordinary workers’ support; shared insecurity and reluctance to leave home also explain the departmental armies’ poor recruitment and collapse. Marseilles’s example spread unevenly through the Midi, while some frontier cities declined to commit.
required_access_facets.stance: The label 'Federalist' is retained as a contested contemporary label; the movement generally defended a unified republic and local autonomy, was geographically narrower than panic suggested, and failed through division and weak military commitment. Neither a purely bourgeois class reaction nor a single royalist plan captures the temporary coalitions; the eight-department contemporary assessment is a corrective to inflated claims rather than an exact timeless measure.

before_fields.meaning: Danton and Desmoulins were eliminated after the Hébertists despite weak evidence of a concrete current conspiracy, because their associations, prior moderation, and potential influence made them politically dangerous.

SUBJ-SUCC-488D7D90E0DF.label: Danton and the Indulgents: campaign for moderation and purge
SUBJ-SUCC-488D7D90E0DF.meaning: Danton’s circle challenged excesses of Terror and pressed moderation amid factional maneuver, scandal and debates over emergency government. The governing coalition then prosecuted and executed them.
SUBJ-SUCC-488D7D90E0DF.stance: Preserve the distinction between demands for moderation, personal or factional motives and charges used to justify destruction. Their removal was part of political consolidation, not proof of every accusation.

required_access_facets.label: Danton and the Indulgents, campaign for moderation
required_access_facets.meaning: Danton and associated Indulgents pressed for less bloodshed and tighter central government, attacked autonomous terrorists, and became compromised by Fabre d'Églantine's corruption scandal and factional maneuvering. Desmoulins’s Vieux Cordelier publicized clemency and wrongful-detention claims with initial Robespierrist support. The short-lived committee of justice was abolished through Collot and Billaud’s opposition; Fabre’s fraud compromised the alliance.
required_access_facets.stance: Danton also sponsored emergency coercive measures in September; his later moderation and defense of Fabre did not erase earlier support for terror policy. Danton’s prior sponsorship of coercive measures and defense of compromised friends prevent a simple equation of indulgence with consistent principled innocence.
acceptable_access: Danton and the Indulgents, campaign for moderation

required_access_facets.label: Dantonists and Indulgents, purge and execution
required_access_facets.meaning: The prosecution of Fabre d'Eglantine, Danton, Desmoulins, and associates, including the politically broadened charges and curtailed trial. Amar’s delayed report and divided committees show that turning a corruption case into a political purge was contested. Danton was not himself charged with corruption; a misleading report of prisoner revolt enabled exclusion of defendants who had demanded witnesses.
required_access_facets.stance: The chapter emphasizes the vagueness of the accusations, the lack of reliable evidence for motive, and the purge's role in inaugurating the Republic of Virtue. Their potential influence is the author’s cautious explanation, not a demonstrated current conspiracy or settled account of every actor’s motive.
acceptable_access: Dantonists and Indulgents, purge and execution

required_access_facets.label: The 'Federalist' revolt: character, motives, and limits
required_access_facets.meaning: The dispersed provincial revolts of 1793 joined republican resistance to Parisian and Montagnard domination with local social conflict, property fears, wartime burdens, and limited royalist opportunism. Rich leaders required ordinary workers’ support; shared insecurity and reluctance to leave home also explain the departmental armies’ poor recruitment and collapse. Marseilles’s example spread unevenly through the Midi, while some frontier cities declined to commit.
required_access_facets.stance: The label 'Federalist' is retained as a contested contemporary label; the movement generally defended a unified republic and local autonomy, was geographically narrower than panic suggested, and failed through division and weak military commitment. Neither a purely bourgeois class reaction nor a single royalist plan captures the temporary coalitions; the eight-department contemporary assessment is a corrective to inflated claims rather than an exact timeless measure.

before_fields.label: Federalist revolts: collapse and differentiated repression
before_fields.meaning: The rapid or protracted defeat of the heterogeneous provincial revolts labeled Federalist and the sharply unequal punishments imposed afterward.
before_fields.stance: Preserve Doyle's quotation-marked and differentiated usage: these movements were not one coherent ideological or military bloc, and Paris treated them very differently.

SUBJ-SUCC-2599FEAE9CC2.label: Marseilles and Bordeaux, surrender and comparatively moderate repression
SUBJ-SUCC-2599FEAE9CC2.meaning: Military pressure and subsistence crisis ended resistance in Marseilles and Bordeaux, where later tribunals and commissions were markedly less lethal than at Lyons, Toulon, or Nantes. Marseilles’s bread blockade divided resistance before military collapse. Bordeaux moved from early rhetorical resistance to restoration of the Convention’s authority; Tallien’s relative moderation was followed by Jullien’s much more intense late repression. Preserve Sansnom and Bec d’Ambès as symbolic names.
SUBJ-SUCC-2599FEAE9CC2.stance: Comparative moderation does not mean absence of executions, and Bordeaux became harsher under Jullien in 1794. Provincial defeat did not produce uniform repression: conciliation at Caen and later policy changes contextualize contrasting local outcomes.
acceptable_access: Marseilles and Bordeaux, surrender and comparatively moderate repression

SUBJ-SUCC-F4D91D47A532.label: Directory: political balance, loss of legitimacy and collapse
SUBJ-SUCC-F4D91D47A532.meaning: The regime sought a propertied republican centre between royalism and Jacobinism through manipulation, coups, military dependence and alternating alliances. Fiscal reconstruction alienated supporters while exclusion of legitimate opposition hollowed out representative practice.
SUBJ-SUCC-F4D91D47A532.stance: The constitution was not simply doomed by design: political actors refused to let it operate freely. Threats from both extremes were real, but repeated preemption destroyed trust and abstention cannot be read as positive consent.
acceptable_access: Party politics -- rejection under the Directory

required_access_facets.label: Directory, political character and instability, 1795-1799
required_access_facets.meaning: The Directory as a property-based republican middle way that sought stability between Jacobinism and royalism but repeatedly overrode constitutional government and became dependent on military power.
required_access_facets.stance: The regime alternately cultivated and repressed left and right, seeking a propertied republican middle way. Its coups expressed failure to trust its constitution; fiscal reconstruction alienated its intended supporters. Renewed war, religious coercion, and conscription recalled earlier revolutionary conflicts without making the Directory identical to the Year II.

required_access_facets.label: Failure of the Directory, Constitution of Year III, and representative politics
required_access_facets.meaning: The chapter's structural explanation for the Directory's collapse: repeated electoral manipulation, mistrust of voters, rejection of party politics, and irreconcilable royalist and Jacobin opposition.
required_access_facets.stance: The constitution was not given a genuine trial: political manipulation and rejection of legitimate organized opposition destroyed its credibility. The Directors failed to organize their own centre and alternately suppressed parties. Yet royalist and Jacobin threats were real; critique of repression is not proof that either extreme would tolerate pluralism.
acceptable_access: Party politics -- rejection under the Directory
Royalist and Jacobin intolerance of opposition

SUBJ-SUCC-B3198138AEB7.stance: Presented as effective state rebuilding through methods and taxes reminiscent of the old regime, producing slow results and increased hostility among propertied citizens.

before_fields.label: Five-member Directory and rotating executive
before_fields.meaning: Executive power is vested in five Directors chosen through the two Councils, with one member retiring annually.
before_fields.stance: Preserve the indirect selection, collective structure, and rotation designed to prevent personal dictatorship.

SUBJ-SUCC-CB77C5EDB693.label: Constitution of the Year III
SUBJ-SUCC-CB77C5EDB693.meaning: The Year III constitution replaced the unused 1793 design with civil rights balanced by duties and a property-based account of political competence. Taxpayer primary voters chose a narrower property-qualified electoral college; bicameral Councils, a five-member rotating executive, separation of powers, and an exceptionally slow amendment process were designed to preserve 1789 and block both political extremes.
SUBJ-SUCC-CB77C5EDB693.stance: Civil equality was accepted while social or absolute equality was rejected. Distinguish primary voting from the restricted body choosing deputies. These were substantive choices about power, not merely procedural details; the Second Directory retained the restricted franchise despite tactical reliance on the left.

before_fields.label: Flight to Varennes
before_fields.meaning: Whole-book synthesis: Louis XVI and his family attempted to leave Paris for the eastern frontier under arrangements made through Fersen and Bouillé, but delays, public suspicion, and recognition led to their arrest at Varennes. The failed royal flight revealed Louis XVI’s repudiation of the Revolution, encouraged republicanism and officer emigration, and pushed European courts and émigrés toward military intervention.
before_fields.stance: Preserve the combined source qualifications: The author identifies Varennes as the Revolution’s second great turning point, exposing the king’s rejection of the settlement and forcing choices over monarchy, republicanism, and war. Emphasize consequences rather than attributing the operation to Artois or the émigré command, which lacked advance control.
acceptable_access: Flight to Varennes: effect on counter-revolution

SUBJ-SUCC-6216510D2EE3.label: Flight to Varennes: royal rejection and domestic and European consequences
SUBJ-SUCC-6216510D2EE3.meaning: The attempted escape of the royal family toward the frontier failed through delays, recognition and local action. It exposed the king’s rejection of the revolutionary settlement, divided constitutional and republican opinion, accelerated officer emigration, and changed foreign calculations.
SUBJ-SUCC-6216510D2EE3.stance: The author treats Varennes as a major turning point. Preserve the royal operation’s independence from émigré control and distinguish its domestic consequences from foreign rulers’ still-conditional response.
acceptable_access: Flight to Varennes—impact on European monarchs and governments

required_access_facets.label: Flight to Varennes

SUBJ-SUCC-8A64FF09886C.meaning: Subsistence demands and inflation forced controls over grain, prices, wages and supply. Enforcement and purchasing constraints altered relations between the government, producers, traders and workers; Thermidorian repeal returned toward a free market amid renewed deprivation.
SUBJ-SUCC-8A64FF09886C.stance: Distinguish price from wage control, formal ceilings from availability, and popular pressure from governmental priorities. Controls did not uniformly benefit workers, and abolition did not by itself restore plenty.

required_access_facets.label: Economic crisis, popular subsistence demands, and the maximum
required_access_facets.meaning: Currency depreciation, scarcity, blockade, requisitioning, and soaring prices drove popular price-setting and demands for legal controls, reshaping factional alliances. Preserve women-led just-price action in Paris in February and June and in Lyons in May as concrete forms of protest. The May law concerned grain and bread; proposals for comprehensive controls and the July capital law against hoarding had different scopes.
required_access_facets.stance: The source treats popular action as grounded in real subsistence pressures while noting pillage and violence; Montagnard support for controls was a political turning point rather than an immediate cure. Distinguish popular price-setting from outright pillage and the limited May maximum from broader demands.
acceptable_access: Economic crisis, popular subsistence demands, and the maximum
maximum - economic crisis and price controls

required_access_facets.label: General Maximum and controlled provisioning: limits and political effects
required_access_facets.meaning: The General Maximum imposed national price controls and penalties but encountered local implementation failures, evasion, black markets, and political constraints on wage controls. Milling drought, currency decline and bread scarcity gave subsistence protests a material basis. The national Subsistence Commission under Lindet revised prices for transport and profit; regional variation, black markets and army purchasing obstructed control. Wage ceilings were largely unenforced because administration was costly and workers were politically indispensable.
required_access_facets.stance: The law had real stabilizing effects but never eliminated market disruption and was not uniformly enforced. Distinguish the September General Maximum from the earlier limited grain maximum and the capital law against hoarding. Assignat recovery was substantial but temporary, and controlled provisioning was incomplete.
acceptable_access: General Maximum and controlled provisioning: limits and political effects

required_access_facets.label: Maximum, wage controls, and workers
required_access_facets.meaning: The government's pre- and post-Thermidor use of the maximum to control wages and prices, and workers' resistance to falling real earnings. The Le Chapelier Law punishes tobacco workers’ agitation and threatened war-worker conscription supplies another disciplinary instrument. In August harsher wage schedules are replaced by more generous rates; this is not removal of every legal wage schedule.
required_access_facets.stance: The maximum restrains inflation imperfectly but its new wage schedule sharply cuts workers' real earnings and helps alienate Paris sections from the Robespierrists.

required_access_facets.label: Abolition of the Maximum and return toward a free market
required_access_facets.meaning: The Thermidorian retreat from price controls and its intended and actual economic consequences.
required_access_facets.stance: The deputies accept claims that controls worsened scarcity, but abolition amid shortages produces severe price rises and destabilizes state finance.
acceptable_access: Abolition of the Maximum and return toward a free market

before_fields.meaning: The steeply progressive levy on higher incomes that removed depreciated assignats from circulation and symbolized class-directed emergency finance.

SUBJ-SUCC-5DD90C556A55.label: Forced loan and Ventôse decrees: distinct emergency property measures
SUBJ-SUCC-5DD90C556A55.meaning: The progressive forced loan retired depreciated assignats and was remembered as class legislation, although uneven implementation and payment in paper softened its burden. required_access_facets.label: Revolutionary Government, creation and centralization
required_access_facets.meaning: Emergency government evolved from a formally limited Committee of Public Safety into a centralized revolutionary state directing administration, police, and enforcement while remaining under the Convention. The Law of 14 Frimaire made the Convention paramount, required district and commune reports through national agents, bypassed departmental political authority and abolished local armies. Robespierre distinguished temporary revolutionary government from constitutional protection.
required_access_facets.stance: Do not equate the Committee with an uncontested conventional executive; the source stresses both its growing practical leadership and the Convention's overriding authority. Administrative implementation took months; Javogues resisted recall, and formal centralization is not proof of instantaneous obedience.

SUBJ-SUCC-3F2B224B895F.label: Jacobins under the Directory: repeated revival, containment and repression
SUBJ-SUCC-3F2B224B895F.meaning: Clubs, press, constitutional circles and parliamentary campaigns revived in successive crises from 1795 to 1799. Governmental indulgence and subsidies alternated with closure, harassment and repression when mobilization threatened the propertied middle course.
SUBJ-SUCC-3F2B224B895F.stance: Pantheon, constitutional circles and Manège were distinct formations. Wartime emergency and anti-royalism created opportunities, but neither official encouragement nor electoral gains meant stable Jacobin control.

required_access_facets.label: Jacobins under the Directory: revival, controlled mobilization, and repression
required_access_facets.meaning: In 1795–1796 official indulgence and subsidies aided the press and Pantheon Club before closures and purges forced radicals underground. After Fructidor the constitutional circles rallied anti-royalists, then again faced restriction when demands for democracy and wider suffrage escaped government control.
required_access_facets.stance: The two cycles illustrate tactical use without empowerment of the left. Neither Jacobins nor constitutional circles were a uniform organization; distinguish Babouvist conspiracy, broad republican mobilization, and later parliamentary ambitions.

required_access_facets.label: Jacobin resurgence and emergency politics in 1799
required_access_facets.meaning: The post-Prairial revival of Jacobin newspapers, clubs, officeholding, and emergency legislation during renewed military danger, followed by Sieyes's containment of the movement.
required_access_facets.stance: The resurgence was real but did not command a parliamentary majority. Wartime emergency and memories of Year II magnified fear; Sieyes’s containment served his own executive project. Rejection of Jourdan’s Country in Danger motion marks the limit of renewed emergency government.

SUBJ-SUCC-13D741A01D65.label: Coup of 18 Brumaire and fall of the Directory
SUBJ-SUCC-13D741A01D65.meaning: The November 1799 coup that transferred the Councils to Saint-Cloud, used military force to disperse the Five Hundred, ended the Directory, and installed a provisional Consulate.
SUBJ-SUCC-13D741A01D65.stance: The coup nearly failed in the chambers and succeeded through deception, military coercion, and a compliant remnant of the legislature rather than orderly constitutional consent.

SUBJ-SUCC-72A1D9C70157.label: Dechristianization, spread, resistance, and decline
SUBJ-SUCC-72A1D9C70157.meaning: Locally initiated attacks on Catholic practice became Paris Commune policy and a nationwide movement, provoked resistance, and helped drive the Committee toward centralization and formal protection of worship. Provincial initiatives spread through Parisian ceremony and church closure; clerical renunciation often involved coercion, including constitutional clergy. Popular resistance in Brie and Robespierre’s appeal to social order encouraged the December freedom-of-cults decree.
SUBJ-SUCC-72A1D9C70157.stance: The movement was not initially authorized by the Convention and remained uneven; the source treats its excesses as politically counterproductive rather than as a uniform state plan. Legal protection of worship did not immediately reopen churches or end persecution. Grégoire’s resistance qualifies claims of universal clerical submission.
acceptable_access: Robespierre, Maximilien > religion and Supreme Being

SUBJ-SUCC-9DC759EBDD0D.label: Church and State, separation and restoration of worship
SUBJ-SUCC-9DC759EBDD0D.meaning: The end of the constitutional Church, formal separation of Church and State, freedom of worship, and practical reopening of churches. The September withdrawal of cult funding precedes February permission for self-financed worship. Clerical dress, public ceremonies and bells remain prohibited. Ending western religious grievances is an explicit strategic motive.
SUBJ-SUCC-9DC759EBDD0D.stance: The settlement abandons state-sponsored civic religion and seeks to reconcile Catholics without restoring public funding or unrestricted religious display. Formal privatization does not mean every locality instantly obeyed restrictions; reported services illustrate religious revival, not restored state establishment.

SUBJ-SUCC-2E013F69DF56.label: Lille negotiations, Fructidor, and the hardening of French peace terms
SUBJ-SUCC-2E013F69DF56.meaning: British peace efforts developed from the failed 1796 mission to Lille in 1797 as Pitt adapted to allied defeats and strategic stalemate. Royalist and moderate gains initially offered room for compromise; Fructidor removed them and hardened French terms. Britain accepted French European gains but rejected uncompensated restitution of Dutch and Spanish colonial captures as well as French possessions.
SUBJ-SUCC-2E013F69DF56.stance: Pitt’s willingness to negotiate was real but bounded by remaining maritime strength; the breakdown cannot be reduced to ideological refusal of peace.
acceptable_access: Lille negotiations, Fructidor, and the hardening of French peace terms

before_fields.label: French Revolution as the first modern and archetypal revolution
before_fields.meaning: The Revolution became the dominant model of modern political transformation, shattering inherited acceptance and placing every later European order in its shadow.
before_fields.stance: Even after 1917 its claim to primacy remains strong, although some developments credited to it were continuations of older trends.

SUBJ-SUCC-251A2CCA89B2.label: The French Revolution as modern archetype and cultural tragedy
SUBJ-SUCC-251A2CCA89B2.meaning: The Revolution became a model of deliberate political transformation and altered political culture, memory and imagined human agency. The author’s final assessment weighs courage and Enlightenment idealism against institutional destruction, mass death, and ruined lives in France and abroad.
SUBJ-SUCC-251A2CCA89B2.stance: Preserve the double judgment: inspiring and ennobling yet appalling and tragic. Aggregate mortality and nonfatal suffering are central to the verdict. The closing figures are the author’s broad estimates, not an independent verified demographic calculation, and the argument does not reduce the Revolution to either triumph or failure.

before_fields.label: French revolutionary expansion and forced republicanization
before_fields.meaning: Whole-book synthesis: French victories, expatriate activism, clubs, and annexations convinced many Europeans that France intended to revolutionize and republicanize the continent by force. The chapter maps and narrates a layered European order composed of France proper, annexed departments, military occupations, and formally separate client republics.
before_fields.stance: Preserve the combined source qualifications: The perception persisted even after France withdrew its open-ended fraternity pledge, so perceived intent exceeded consistent official policy. Territorial form varied with strategy and diplomacy, but every form enlarged French power and exposed the contradiction between revolutionary liberation and domination.
acceptable_access: French revolutionary expansion and forced republicanization
Revolutionary French expansion: annexations, occupations, and sister republics

required_access_facets.label: Great Nation ideology and French expansionism

required_access_facets.label: Occupied Europe under revolutionary French rule, 1794-1799
required_access_facets.meaning: The chapter-wide transformation of conquered or coerced European territories through annexation, military occupation, and dependent republican regimes.
required_access_facets.stance: Annexations, occupations and dependent republics took different constitutional forms. French liberty increasingly meant French national control, unable to accommodate other traditions of freedom. Extraction and intervention reduced foreign support and multiplied enemies; this is a qualified argument about domination, not a claim that all reform or native cooperation was absent.

required_access_facets.label: Economic crisis, popular subsistence demands, and the maximum
required_access_facets.meaning: Currency depreciation, scarcity, blockade, requisitioning, and soaring prices drove popular price-setting and demands for legal controls, reshaping factional alliances. Preserve women-led just-price action in Paris in February and June and in Lyons in May as concrete forms of protest. The May law concerned grain and bread; proposals for comprehensive controls and the July capital law against hoarding had different scopes.
required_access_facets.stance: The source treats popular action as grounded in real subsistence pressures while noting pillage and violence; Montagnard support for controls was a political turning point rather than an immediate cure. Distinguish popular price-setting from outright pillage and the limited May maximum from broader demands.

required_access_facets.label: General Maximum and controlled provisioning: limits and political effects
required_access_facets.meaning: The General Maximum imposed national price controls and penalties but encountered local implementation failures, evasion, black markets, and political constraints on wage controls. Milling drought, currency decline and bread scarcity gave subsistence protests a material basis. The national Subsistence Commission under Lindet revised prices for transport and profit; regional variation, black markets and army purchasing obstructed control. Wage ceilings were largely unenforced because administration was costly and workers were politically indispensable.
required_access_facets.stance: The law had real stabilizing effects but never eliminated market disruption and was not uniformly enforced. Distinguish the September General Maximum from the earlier limited grain maximum and the capital law against hoarding. Assignat recovery was substantial but temporary, and controlled provisioning was incomplete.
acceptable_access: General Maximum and controlled provisioning: limits and political effects

required_access_facets.label: Maximum, wage controls, and workers
required_access_facets.meaning: The government's pre- and post-Thermidor use of the maximum to control wages and prices, and workers' resistance to falling real earnings. The Le Chapelier Law punishes tobacco workers’ agitation and threatened war-worker conscription supplies another disciplinary instrument. In August harsher wage schedules are replaced by more generous rates; this is not removal of every legal wage schedule.
required_access_facets.stance: The maximum restrains inflation imperfectly but its new wage schedule sharply cuts workers' real earnings and helps alienate Paris sections from the Robespierrists.

required_access_facets.label: Abolition of the Maximum and return toward a free market
required_access_facets.meaning: The Thermidorian retreat from price controls and its intended and actual economic consequences.
required_access_facets.stance: The deputies accept claims that controls worsened scarcity, but abolition amid shortages produces severe price rises and destabilizes state finance.

required_access_facets.label: The 'Federalist' revolt: character, motives, and limits
required_access_facets.meaning: The dispersed provincial revolts of 1793 joined republican resistance to Parisian and Montagnard domination with local social conflict, property fears, wartime burdens, and limited royalist opportunism. Rich leaders required ordinary workers’ support; shared insecurity and reluctance to leave home also explain the departmental armies’ poor recruitment and collapse. Marseilles’s example spread unevenly through the Midi, while some frontier cities declined to commit.
required_access_facets.stance: The label 'Federalist' is retained as a contested contemporary label; the movement generally defended a unified republic and local autonomy, was geographically narrower than panic suggested, and failed through division and weak military commitment. Neither a purely bourgeois class reaction nor a single royalist plan captures the temporary coalitions; the eight-department contemporary assessment is a corrective to inflated claims rather than an exact timeless measure.

After its failure Pichegru receives security command, former committee leaders are sentenced to deportation, ex-Montagnards are arrested and the 10 April disarmament law exposes former activists to reprisals.
required_access_facets.stance: The action expresses acute subsistence distress but lacks a clear program, coordination, durable institutions, or decisive armed support. The demonstration’s failure and the subsequent wider purge are separate stages; some local counter-terror predates the law.
acceptable_access: Germinal uprising and its punitive aftermath

before_fields.label: Muscadins and Gilded Youth in anti-sans-culotte politics
before_fields.meaning: Better-off, conspicuously styled young opponents of sans-culotte politics moved from sectional opposition to organized street violence against popular institutions, Jacobins, former terrorists, and revolutionary symbols.
before_fields.stance: The Muscadins or Gilded Youth formed a mixed private political force rather than a simply aristocratic or uniformly royalist body, and their role changed with the Thermidorian balance of power.
acceptable_access: Muscadins and Gilded Youth in anti-sans-culotte politics

SUBJ-SUCC-65D590EBAFE2.label: Paris, the provinces, and national sovereignty
SUBJ-SUCC-65D590EBAFE2.meaning: The Convention's dependence on Parisian popular power made the constitutional relation between the capital, elected national representatives, and the departments the chapter's central conflict. Sections and the democratized National Guard supplied coercive power, but Paris was internally divided: Muscadins briefly captured several sectional assemblies. Departmental-guard proposals sought protection for national deliberation; the same sectional forms served opposing provincial coalitions.
SUBJ-SUCC-65D590EBAFE2.stance: Paris created and protected the Republic but could also coerce its representatives; provincial resistance claimed to defend national representation and local autonomy rather than simply to reject republican unity. An urban section was not inherently Montagnard, and indivisible-republic rhetoric was shared by competing camps.

SUBJ-SUCC-ED09FB8A7BAE.label: Jacobin Club, Gilded Youth, and anti-Jacobin reaction
SUBJ-SUCC-ED09FB8A7BAE.meaning: The organized street and political campaign against Jacobins, culminating in closure of the Paris Jacobin Club. Membership publication and a ban on interclub correspondence undermine the affiliate network before closure. The Gilded Youth mixes ex-prisoners, draft dodgers, clerks and petty officials, then serves as an informal legislative guard.
SUBJ-SUCC-ED09FB8A7BAE.stance: The campaign combines genuine reaction against terror with intimidation and violence that the Convention ultimately ratifies. Conspicuous dress does not establish that all participants were aristocrats or royalists.

before_fields.meaning: Personal, constitutional, economic, and wartime disputes progressively organize Convention politics into antagonistic camps.

SUBJ-SUCC-86D03B0C3585.label: Girondins and Montagnards: principles, organization and predominance
SUBJ-SUCC-86D03B0C3585.meaning: Overlapping Girondin circles defended the principles of 1789, national consultation and freedom from Parisian coercion, while the Mountain adapted to war and popular pressure and usually assembled majorities. The king’s trial, shifting war policy, Jacobin expulsions and memories of September deepened conflict; the Plain reluctantly chose among them.
SUBJ-SUCC-86D03B0C3585.stance: Neither modern two-party competition nor overthrow of a Girondin government explains 2 June. Girondin intransigence contrasted with Montagnard pragmatism; most of their principles were widely shared, and removal of leading speakers clarified existing control.

SUBJ-SUCC-8E3A7F5371C6.label: Commission of Twelve and the insurrections of 31 May–2 June 1793
SUBJ-SUCC-8E3A7F5371C6.meaning: A divided and initially ineffective uprising on 31 May was followed by overwhelming National Guard pressure on 2 June, forcing arrests of deputies and ministers. before_fields.meaning: The compressed show trial and execution of leading Girondins, imprisonment of protest signatories, and deaths of fugitives outside Paris.
before_fields.stance: The central proceeding was designed to avoid prolonged defense, but Robespierre resisted extending capital prosecution to every deputy associated with the purge protest.

SUBJ-SUCC-C946EBBA6629.label: Political trials and executions in Paris, autumn 1793
SUBJ-SUCC-C946EBBA6629.meaning: The trials and executions of Marie-Antoinette, leading Girondins, and other prominent figures gave the Terror famous public victims while masking its predominantly provincial toll. The queen’s rescue plot made further postponement difficult; leading Girondins faced an accelerated show trial, while Robespierre resisted prosecuting all protesting deputies. The later Hébertist trial again subordinated defense to the desired result.
SUBJ-SUCC-C946EBBA6629.stance: Treat the trials as politically managed and symbolically prominent, not numerically representative of the Terror's victims. Famous Parisian victims disproportionately shaped memory; they do not represent the Terror’s typical geography or social composition.
acceptable_access: Political trials and executions in Paris, autumn 1793

SUBJ-SUCC-5193E3F37320.label: Assignats: land-backed origins, paper currency, inflation and redistribution
SUBJ-SUCC-5193E3F37320.meaning: Nationalized land supported an initial bond scheme that became circulating paper. Over-issue, fiscal weakness and war drove depreciation, altered national-land sale returns and redistributed resources among debtors, creditors, wage earners and purchasers.
SUBJ-SUCC-5193E3F37320.stance: Distinguish the original retirement-through-land-sales plan from later monetary practice. War intensified rather than alone caused depreciation; nominal payment or cheap acquisition cannot be treated as equivalent real value.

required_access_facets.label: Assignats, inflation, and fiscal breakdown
required_access_facets.meaning: The accelerating depreciation of assignats and weakening state finance during the winter and spring of 1794-1795.
required_access_facets.stance: Currency collapse is presented as both a cause and consequence of market liberalization, harvest shortage, and wartime procurement needs.

required_access_facets.label: Assignats, inflation, and redistribution between debtors and creditors
required_access_facets.meaning: Over-issued land-backed assignats depreciated severely, undermining land-sale returns, credit, fixed incomes, wages, production, and employment.
required_access_facets.stance: War intensified the monetary collapse, but fiscal weakness and revolutionary over-issue caused most depreciation and broad economic damage.

required_access_facets.label: Assignats: final collapse and abandonment
required_access_facets.meaning: Further depreciation, failed emergency levies and opposition to a land bank culminated in the end of assignat printing. Symbolic destruction of the plates did not itself restore finance.
required_access_facets.stance: Distinguish the ending of assignat production from the later failure of mandates and the deflation caused by scarce metallic currency.

SUBJ-SUCC-F6EDFC76AB9A.label: Territorial mandates and post-paper deflation
SUBJ-SUCC-F6EDFC76AB9A.meaning: Land-backed mandates rapidly depreciated and facilitated property speculation before losing legal-tender status and being demonetized. Scarce specie then brought falling prices, high interest, pressure on debtors and barter.
SUBJ-SUCC-F6EDFC76AB9A.stance: A new name and land backing did not stabilize paper. Ending paper money replaced inflation with a different crisis rather than normal monetary conditions.

required_access_facets.meaning: The complex electoral framework of bailliages and senechaussees, grouped districts, separately represented towns, provincial exceptions, and order-specific assemblies.

before_fields.stance: The alleged conspiracy charges were manufactured for a political result, yet the movement's organizational weakness and reckless insurrectionary rhetoric were real.
acceptable_access: Hébertists: failed insurrection and political execution

SUBJ-SUCC-7FD46BD9C318.label: Hébert and the Hébertists, rise and destruction
SUBJ-SUCC-7FD46BD9C318.meaning: Hébert's circle appropriated radical subsistence and terror policies, led popular pressure and dechristianization, defended provincial terror, then failed to mobilize an insurrection and was destroyed in a political trial. Hébert’s Père Duchesne, Ronsin’s army command and Vincent’s war-ministry role connected journalism and coercive institutions. Only section Marat answered the March insurrection call. Foreign-born defendants, including Clootz, supplied theatrical support for the constructed foreign-plot charge.
SUBJ-SUCC-7FD46BD9C318.stance: The label Hébertists is presented as a contemporary or retrospective factional designation; membership and alleged foreign conspiracy were not firmly established. Real organizational weakness and provocative calls for a purge must be separated from the fabricated famine and massacre conspiracy used at trial.
acceptable_access: Hébert and the Hébertists, rise and destruction
Hébert, Jacques-René > radical politics and execution

before_fields.label: Helvetic Republic and French control
before_fields.meaning: Whole-book synthesis: A French-backed coup replaces the Swiss Confederation with a centralized sister republic that grants France permanent access through the Alps. French authorities and Swiss reformers Peter Ochs and Frédéric-César de La Harpe replaced the loose Confederation with a centralized republic whose constitution copied French institutions.
before_fields.stance: Preserve the combined source qualifications: Treat the Helvetic settlement as strategic coercion and state transformation, not simply voluntary republican imitation. The author acknowledges domestic reform initiative but emphasizes that French invasion, coercion, and imposition without national ratification made the new state dependent from birth.
acceptable_access: Helvetic Republic and French control of the Alpine passes
Helvetic Republic: imposed unity and constrained sovereignty

SUBJ-SUCC-2FE1E44C6B8E.label: Sister republics: creation, constitutional diversity and constrained sovereignty
SUBJ-SUCC-2FE1E44C6B8E.meaning: French-sponsored states spread through military and diplomatic expansion, with varying local initiative, constitutional authorship and domestic autonomy. Strategic access, occupation, financial obligations and repeated interventions limited sovereignty.
SUBJ-SUCC-2FE1E44C6B8E.stance: Do not flatten Dutch or Ligurian local initiative into the same model as imposed Swiss unity or Roman military supremacy. The Directory did not uniformly welcome every new satellite, but their spread deepened international alarm.

required_access_facets.label: Sister republics under the Directory
required_access_facets.meaning: French creation or sponsorship of the Helvetic, Roman, and Parthenopean republics as instruments and consequences of expansion.
required_access_facets.stance: The republics are presented as imposed, dependent, and often unstable; the Directory did not uniformly welcome every new puppet regime, but their creation deepened international alarm.

required_access_facets.label: Sister republics as dependent French client states
required_access_facets.meaning: The Batavian, Helvetic, Cisalpine, Ligurian, Roman, and Parthenopean republics as constitutional experiments constrained by French strategic and fiscal priorities.
required_access_facets.stance: Client institutions varied substantially: Dutch elections and relative domestic autonomy, locally drafted Ligurian institutions, imposed Swiss unity, and the Roman commandant’s explicit supremacy must not be flattened into identical puppets. Military dependence and French interference qualified all these experiments.

SUBJ-SUCC-F15AB2809FA2.label: Helvetic Republic: French intervention and imposed constitution
SUBJ-SUCC-F15AB2809FA2.meaning: The strategic origins, invasion, creation, and imposed centralized constitution of the Helvetic Republic in 1798.
SUBJ-SUCC-F15AB2809FA2.stance: French strategic needs and Swiss reformers' centralizing plans overrode older cantonal freedoms and local aims.

required_access_facets.meaning: The strategic origins, invasion, creation, and imposed centralized constitution of the Helvetic Republic in 1798.
required_access_facets.stance: French strategic needs and Swiss reformers' centralizing plans overrode older cantonal freedoms and local aims.

before_fields.label: Heterogeneous and propertied composition of the Vendémiaire opposition
before_fields.meaning: Many Vendémiaire participants were people of property seeking security, and their royalism was not established uniformly.
before_fields.stance: Do not label the entire uprising royalist; retain the government's strategic hope of winning substantial citizens back to the constitution.
acceptable_access: Heterogeneous and propertied composition of the Vendémiaire opposition

SUBJ-SUCC-56435A176677.label: Vendémiaire uprising, 1795
SUBJ-SUCC-56435A176677.meaning: The Paris sectional insurrection against the Two Thirds Law, its military defeat under Barras with Bonaparte's advice, and its constitutional consequences.
SUBJ-SUCC-56435A176677.stance: Treated as a more important turning point than the formal inauguration of the Directory because it ended Parisian coercion of national representatives and established military force as decisive in domestic politics; the text cautions that most participants were not demonstrably royalist.
